title: When Emotions Become Physical
text:
A measured question, not a simple answer



What does a self-reported symptom scale have to do with a blood marker? This comparison offers a careful starting point.

title: When Emotions Become Physical
text:
The share above 3 mg/L
Each bar is the percentage of participants in that PHQ-9 symptom group whose hs-CRP was above 3 mg/L. Denominators are shown below the group labels; values describe this complete-case sample, not the U.S. population.









The question here is whether the proportion above a commonly used hs-CRP threshold differs across PHQ-9 symptom groups in adults who completed all the selected NHANES measures. The PHQ-9 asks about nine symptoms over the previous two weeks; it is a screening measure, not a diagnosis or a complete account of someone’s emotional life.
In this sample, the observed proportions range from 33.6% to 50.0% across groups. The group denominators shown on the chart matter: the more severe symptom categories can have fewer participants, so their percentages may be less stable. These figures are unweighted descriptions, not adjusted estimates for all U.S. adults.
A 2026 NHANES analysis by Arellano and colleagues examined hs-CRP and depression symptom severity using multivariable methods. That peer-reviewed work provides context, but this project uses a complete-case subset and does not apply survey weights or reproduce its adjusted analyses. A separate 2024 cross-sectional study also examines hs-CRP alongside depressive symptoms.
NHANES is observational and these measurements do not establish which came first, explain an association, or rule out other factors. hs-CRP is a nonspecific marker of inflammation—not a measure of immune strength, emotional experience as a whole, or how quickly a person recovers.

i

Interpret with care

Group-level percentages cannot diagnose individuals. This visualization does not measure immune function or healing speed, and it does not support a cause-and-effect conclusion.

title: The Mind–Immunity Connection
text:
A closer look at health, mood & inflammation



Exploring the relationship between depressive symptoms and inflammation in U.S. adults.


Could depressive symptoms and a marker of inflammation appear together in a national health survey? We explored this question using real participant data from the 2017–2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES).

Explore the evidence →

title: The Mind–Immunity Connection
text:
One dot, one participant
Each point below represents one complete adult NHANES participant. The horizontal position is their PHQ-9 symptom score; the vertical position is their hs-CRP concentration. Overlapping points are made visible with slight jitter and transparency. The vertical axis uses a log10 scale; hover over a point for age, sex, score, and concentration.

title: The Mind–Immunity Connection
text:
A marker, not a verdict
Inflammation is part of the body’s response to injury and infection. C-reactive protein is produced by the liver, and hs-CRP is a sensitive blood measure of this protein. It can be associated with many conditions and circumstances; one measurement does not describe someone’s whole immune system.
This plot shows how two measured values sit alongside one another in this sample. It cannot establish why either value is higher or lower, predict an individual’s health, or show that one causes the other.

title: About
text:
Data source
This project uses adult participant data from the 2017–2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), conducted by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The analysis joins the demographics, depression screener, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein records. See How We Measured It for the selection rules, measures, and limitations.

title: How We Measured It
text:
Transparent data, reproducible steps



Every participant shown comes from original CDC NHANES files. The preparation script downloads, joins, validates, and cleans these source records.

title: How We Measured It
text:
Source and population
The data come from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), 2017–2018. We joined the demographics (DEMO_J), depression screener (DPQ_J), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (HSCRP_J) files using the participant sequence number SEQN. The analytic population is adults aged 20 years or older with reported sex, valid responses to all nine selected PHQ items, and a nonmissing hs-CRP result.
The final dataset contains 4,537 complete adult participants. This count reflects the actual joined records after exclusions; no participants were added, duplicated, or simulated.

title: How We Measured It
text:
Measures and definitions
The nine questions DPQ010 through DPQ090 each use valid response codes 0–3. We excluded any record with a missing response or an invalid item code (7 or 9), then summed the nine valid responses for a total PHQ-9 score from 0 to 27:



Score

The laboratory variable LBXHSCRP is reported in mg/L. For this descriptive analysis, elevated hs-CRP is defined as a value greater than 3 mg/L; a value equal to 3 is not counted as elevated. Age groups in the interactive view are 20–39, 40–59, and 60 years or older. Sex categories follow the NHANES RIAGENDR coding (female or male).

title: How We Measured It
text:
What the numbers mean
The charts report raw participant-level observations, unweighted counts, medians, and percentages among the complete-case adults used here. They are not survey-weighted estimates and are not adjusted for other characteristics. Missing values are excluded rather than imputed.
PHQ-9 is a self-reported symptom screener, not a clinical diagnosis and not a measure of all emotions. hs-CRP is a nonspecific biomarker of inflammation, not a direct measure of immune strength or recovery speed. As a cross-sectional observational analysis, this project cannot establish causation, direction, or an individual’s likely outcome.
The reproducible download and cleaning code is in scripts/prepare_data.R. It caches the original XPT files under data/raw/ and writes the cleaned CSV plus static-site JSON export to data/processed/.
